aghlabid-dynasty.name: Aghlabid dynasty
aghlabid-dynasty.summary: An Arab dynasty that ruled Ifriqiya from 800 to 909 as nominal Abbasid vassals, also conquering Sicily and parts of southern Italy, before falling to the Fatimids.

ifriqiya.name: Ifriqiya
ifriqiya.summary: A medieval historical region covering today's Tunisia, eastern Algeria and western Libya, whose capital was Qayrawan for most of its history.

rustamid-dynasty.name: Rustamid dynasty
rustamid-dynasty.summary: An Ibadi Muslim dynasty of Persian origin that ruled a theocratic state centered on Tahert in present-day Algeria for a century and a half, until defeated by the Fatimid Caliphate.

tiaret.name: Tiaret (Tahert)
tiaret.summary: A city in northwestern Algeria, historically known as Tahert, located in the Hautes Plaines near the Tell Atlas mountains.

fatimid-caliphate.name: Fatimid Caliphate
fatimid-caliphate.summary: An Isma'ili Shia caliphate ruling North Africa and West Asia from the 10th to 12th centuries CE, claiming descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima, with Egypt as its eventual centre.

zirid-dynasty.name: Zirid dynasty
zirid-dynasty.summary: A Sanhaja Berber dynasty that ruled the central Maghreb from 972 to 1014 and Ifriqiya until 1148, at first as emirs governing in the name of the Fatimid Caliphate.

kairouan.name: Kairouan
kairouan.summary: City in Tunisia founded by the Umayyads around 670, which became an important center of Sunni Islamic scholarship and Quranic learning.

uqba-ibn-nafi.name: Uqba ibn Nafi
uqba-ibn-nafi.summary: Arab general (622–683) who led the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb under the Umayyad Caliphate and is credited with establishing Umayyad rule in North Africa, before dying in battle in 683.

great-mosque-of-kairouan.name: Great Mosque of Kairouan
great-mosque-of-kairouan.summary: One of the largest Islamic monuments in North Africa, founded in 670 CE by Uqba ibn Nafi at the founding of Kairouan and later a model for mosques across the Maghreb.

ribat-of-sousse.name: Ribat of Sousse
ribat-of-sousse.summary: A ribat, or Islamic defensive fortress, in Sousse, Tunisia, likely founded in the 8th century and rebuilt under the Aghlabid dynasty in the early 9th century; the best-preserved of its kind in the region.

ribat-of-monastir.name: Ribat of Monastir
ribat-of-monastir.summary: The oldest ribat, or Islamic defensive fortress, built by Arab conquerors in Monastir, Tunisia, and the city's most prominent monument.

almoravid-dynasty.name: Almoravid dynasty
almoravid-dynasty.summary: Berber Muslim dynasty (1050s-1147) centered in Morocco that built an empire across the western Maghreb and Muslim Spain, founding Marrakesh around 1070.

almohad-caliphate.name: Almohad Caliphate
almohad-caliphate.summary: North African empire ruled by a Berber Muslim dynasty in the 12th and 13th centuries, controlling much of the Maghreb and Islamic Spain at its height.

al-andalus.name: Al-Andalus
al-andalus.summary: The Muslim-ruled territories of the Iberian Peninsula from 711 to 1492, which at their height covered all of Spain and Portugal, with Córdoba becoming a leading cultural and scientific center.

kufic.name: Kufic script
kufic.summary: Angular, early style of Arabic script that developed in the city of Kufa, prized for Quran transcription and architectural decoration.

mihrab.name: Mihrab
mihrab.summary: A niche in a mosque's wall marking the qibla, the direction of Mecca, toward which Muslims face when praying.

al-zaytuna-mosque.name: Al-Zaytuna Mosque
al-zaytuna-mosque.summary: The oldest mosque in Tunis, founded around the 7th–8th century, whose attached school became Tunisia's most important center of higher education.

idrisid-dynasty.name: Idrisid dynasty
idrisid-dynasty.summary: An Arab Muslim dynasty that ruled most of present-day Morocco and parts of western Algeria from 788 to 974, founded by Idris I and central to the early Islamization of Morocco.

fez-morocco.name: Fez
fez-morocco.summary: A city in northern Morocco founded in the 8th century, which became a center of religious scholarship and reached its height under Marinid rule in the 13th to 15th centuries.

mahdia.name: Mahdia
mahdia.summary: A Tunisian coastal city of about 76,500 people, south of Monastir, known for fish processing and weaving and serving as capital of its governorate.

skifa-kahla.name: Skifa Kahla
skifa-kahla.summary: A 10th-century fortified gate, also called Bab Zouila, built by the Fatimids as a main entrance to their new capital, Mahdia, in Tunisia.

squinch.name: Squinch
squinch.summary: An architectural element that supports a round or octagonal dome on a square base, originating in Sassanid Persia and later used in Islamic, Georgian and Armenian buildings.

idris-i-of-morocco.name: Idris I
idris-i-of-morocco.summary: Founder of the Idrisid dynasty in northern Morocco, who ruled from 788 to 791 after fleeing the Hejaz, and is regarded as the founding father of Morocco.

university-of-al-qarawiyyin.name: University of al-Qarawiyyin
university-of-al-qarawiyyin.summary: A university in Fez, Morocco, founded as a mosque in 857–859 and often cited as the oldest continually operating institution of higher learning in the world.

mosque-of-the-andalusians.name: Mosque of the Andalusians
mosque-of-the-andalusians.summary: Historic mosque in Fez, Morocco, founded in 859–860 and one of the country's oldest, named for the Andalusi immigrants of its district.

ribat.name: Ribat
ribat.summary: A small fortification built along Muslim frontiers during the early conquest of the Maghreb to house volunteer soldiers, later also serving as trade-route defenses, community centers and places of piety.

sousse.name: Sousse
sousse.summary: A city in Tunisia on the Gulf of Hammamet, about 140 km south of Tunis, with an economy based on transport equipment, food processing, olive oil, textiles and tourism.

monastir-tunisia.name: Monastir
monastir-tunisia.summary: A coastal city in Tunisia's Sahel region, once a fishing port and now a major tourist resort, and capital of Monastir Governorate.

sfax.name: Sfax
sfax.summary: A major Tunisian port city founded in AD 849, now the country's second-largest city, known for phosphate, olive and fishing industries.

ubayd-allah-ibn-al-habhab.name: Ubayd Allah ibn al-Habhab
ubayd-allah-ibn-al-habhab.summary: Umayyad official who governed Egypt from 724 to 734 and then Kairouan, Ifriqiya from 734 to 741, during whose rule the Great Berber Revolt broke out in North Africa and Iberia.

kahina.name: Al-Kahina
kahina.summary: Amazigh warrior-queen of the Aurès in the 7th century who united Berber tribes against the Muslim conquest, defeating Umayyad forces before her own defeat at the Battle of El Jem.

aur-s.name: Aurès
aur-s.summary: A mountainous natural region in eastern Algeria, spanning several Algerian provinces.

battle-of-meskiana.name: Battle of Meskiana
battle-of-meskiana.summary: A 698 battle in North Africa between Umayyad forces under Hassan ibn al-Nu'man and Queen Dihya.

battle-of-el-jem.name: Battle of El Jem
battle-of-el-jem.summary: A 703 CE battle near El Jem, Tunisia, in which Umayyad forces defeated the Berbers of the Kingdom of the Aurès, ending organized Berber resistance to the caliphate.

berber-revolt.name: Berber Revolt
berber-revolt.summary: A rebellion of Berbers against Umayyad Arab rule in 740–743 CE that began in Tangier, spread across the Maghreb into Al-Andalus, and marked the first successful secession from the Arab Caliphate.

tangier.name: Tangier
tangier.summary: City in northwestern Morocco on the Mediterranean and Atlantic coasts, a Phoenician trading hub turned international zone in 1923 until Moroccan independence.

maysara-al-matghari.name: Maysara al-Matghari
maysara-al-matghari.summary: A Berber rebel leader who launched the Great Berber Revolt against Umayyad rule in 739, only to be deposed and killed by his own followers in 740, three years before their eventual victory.

kharijites.name: Kharijites
kharijites.summary: An Islamic sect that emerged in 656 to 661 among former supporters of Ali who rejected his arbitration with Mu'awiya; their rebellions against Umayyad and later Abbasid rule continued for centuries.

hilderic.name: Hilderic
hilderic.summary: The penultimate king of the Vandals and Alans in North Africa (c. 460-533), ruling 523-530; his deposition by a cousin gave Byzantium a pretext for war.

gelimer.name: Gelimer
gelimer.summary: The last king of the Vandals in North Africa, reigning 530-534, whose defeat by the Byzantine general Belisarius in 533-534 ended the Vandal Kingdom.

vandals.name: Vandals
vandals.summary: A Germanic people who conquered Roman North Africa and ruled it for a century, sacking Rome in 455, until the Byzantine Empire defeated them in 534.

vandalic-war.name: Vandalic War
vandalic-war.summary: A 533-534 war in North Africa in which the Byzantine Empire, led by general Belisarius, conquered the Germanic Vandal Kingdom.

belisarius.name: Belisarius
belisarius.summary: A Byzantine military commander (c. 500-565) under Emperor Justinian I who reconquered North Africa and much of Italy, considered one of history's greatest generals.

abd-allah-ibn-sa-d.name: Abdallah ibn Sa'd
abd-allah-ibn-sa-d.summary: An Arab administrator, scribe and military commander and early convert to Islam who governed Upper Egypt under caliph Uthman and co-founded the Islamic navy that seized Cyprus and defeated a Byzantine fleet.

tripolitania.name: Tripolitania
tripolitania.summary: A historic region of Libya settled since antiquity, ruled in turn by Carthage, Rome, the Vandals, the Byzantines, and Muslim and Ottoman conquerors by the 15th century.

exarchate-of-africa.name: Exarchate of Africa
exarchate-of-africa.summary: A Byzantine province around Carthage covering its Western Mediterranean territories, set up by Emperor Maurice in 591 and ruled by a viceroy called an exarch until the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb.

battle-of-vescera.name: Battle of Vescera
battle-of-vescera.summary: A battle fought in 682 or 683 near modern Biskra, Algeria, where Berber and Byzantine forces ambushed and killed the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi, ending his conquest expedition across North Africa.

battle-of-bagdoura.name: Battle of Bagdoura
battle-of-bagdoura.summary: A decisive Berber victory over Umayyad Arab forces near the Sebou River in late 741 CE, which permanently broke Umayyad control over the far western Maghreb.

battle-of-the-nobles.name: Battle of the Nobles
battle-of-the-nobles.summary: A battle around 740 CE in which Berber rebels under Khalid ibn Hamid al-Zanati defeated Arab forces near Algeria's Chelif River, killing so many Arab aristocrats that it gave the battle its name.

battle-of-al-asnam.name: Battle of al-Asnam
battle-of-al-asnam.summary: A battle in which Umayyad forces under Handhala ibn Safwan al-Kalbi decisively defeated Sufrite Berber rebels, saving Kairouan and Ifriqiya from the revolt.

hassan-ibn-al-nu-man.name: Hassan ibn al-Nu'man
hassan-ibn-al-nu-man.summary: Umayyad Arab general who led the final Muslim conquest of Ifriqiya in the late 7th century, destroying Byzantine Carthage in 698 and founding Tunis the following year.

baghai.name: Baghai
baghai.summary: A town in Khenchela Province, Algeria, with a population of 6,414 as of a 1998 census.

gab-s.name: Gabès
gab-s.summary: Tunisian coastal city, once the Carthaginian and Roman settlement of Tacapae, later an oasis and industrial and commercial hub.

kutama.name: Kutama
kutama.summary: A Berber tribe of northern Algeria that formed the bulk of the Fatimid army, helping overthrow the Aghlabids and go on to conquer Egypt and the southern Levant in 969–975.

abu-abdallah-al-shi-i.name: Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i
abu-abdallah-al-shi-i.summary: Isma'ili missionary who converted and unified the Kutama Berbers, led their conquest of Ifriqiya from 902 to 909, and was executed in 911 after helping found the Fatimid Caliphate.

mu-awiya-i.name: Mu'awiya I
mu-awiya-i.summary: Founder and first caliph of the Umayyad Caliphate, ruling from 661 to 680; a late convert to Islam who rose through the early caliphates before contesting Ali for power.

maliki-school.name: Maliki school
maliki-school.summary: One of the four major Sunni Islamic legal schools, founded by Malik ibn Anas in the 8th century, predominant across North and West Africa and parts of the Gulf.

halakha.name: Halakha
halakha.summary: The collective body of Jewish religious law derived from the Torah and later rabbinic writings, guiding both religious practice and everyday civil life.

abd-al-wahhab-ibn-abd-al-rahman.name: Abd al-Wahhab ibn Abd al-Rahman
abd-al-wahhab-ibn-abd-al-rahman.summary: Second imam of the Imamate of Tahart in Algeria and founder of the Wahbi Ibadism movement, part of the Rustamid dynasty.

aflah-ibn-abd-al-wahhab.name: Aflah ibn Abd al-Wahhab
aflah-ibn-abd-al-wahhab.summary: Third Imam of the Ibadi Rustamid dynasty in the central Maghreb, whose long reign from 823 to 872 is seen as the dynasty's golden age, shaped by the Mu'tazilite movement.

muhammad-ibn-hani-al-andalusi-al-azdi.name: Ibn Hani
muhammad-ibn-hani-al-andalusi-al-azdi.summary: Andalusi poet (c. 936–973) who served as chief court poet to the Fatimid Caliph al-Mu'izz, nicknamed 'al-Mutanabbi of the West', and was murdered on his way from Egypt around 973.

al-mu-izz-li-din-allah.name: al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah
al-mu-izz-li-din-allah.summary: Fourth Fatimid caliph and fourteenth Ismaili imam, reigning 953 to 975, who moved the Fatimid capital from Ifriqiya to Egypt and founded Cairo in 969.

al-mutanabbi.name: al-Mutanabbi
al-mutanabbi.summary: A highly celebrated 10th-century Arab poet (c. 915–965) at the Hamdanid court in Aleppo, regarded as one of the greatest and most influential poets in the Arabic language.

blue-quran.name: Blue Quran
blue-quran.summary: An early Quranic manuscript in Kufic script with gold lettering on rare indigo-dyed parchment, among the most famous works of Islamic calligraphy; its exact date and origin are debated.

nafusa-mountains.name: Nafusa Mountains
nafusa-mountains.summary: A mountain range in northwestern Libya's Tripolitania region, known in Arabic as Jabal Nafusah.

mashriq.name: Mashriq
mashriq.summary: The eastern part of the Arab world, roughly equivalent to 'the Middle East,' as distinguished from the western Maghreb region.

jawhar-general.name: Jawhar al-Siqilli
jawhar-general.summary: A Fatimid general of Byzantine Greek origin from Sicily who conquered the Maghreb and Egypt for Caliph al-Mu'izz, serving as Egypt's viceroy until 973 and dying in 992.

m-sila-algeria.name: M'Sila
m-sila-algeria.summary: Now the capital of M'Sila Province in Algeria, with a population of about 133,000 as of the 2008 census.

qasida.name: Qasida
qasida.summary: An ancient Arabic ode form using a single meter and rhyme throughout, originating in pre-Islamic poetry and later adopted into Persian and Turkish literature.

yahya-ibn-ali-ibn-hammud-al-mu-tali.name: Yahya ibn Ali
yahya-ibn-ali-ibn-hammud-al-mu-tali.summary: Hammudid Caliph of Cordoba in Muslim Spain, ruling in two separate periods between 1021 and 1026.
yahya-ibn-ali-ibn-hammud-al-mu-tali.source_title: Yahya ibn Ali ibn Hammud al-Mu'tali

isaac-israeli-ben-solomon.name: Isaac Israeli ben Solomon
isaac-israeli-ben-solomon.summary: Jewish physician and philosopher (c. 832–c. 932), considered the father of medieval Jewish Neoplatonism, whose Arabic medical works were later translated into Latin and taught in European universities.

ziyadat-allah-iii-of-ifriqiya.name: Ziyadat Allah III
ziyadat-allah-iii-of-ifriqiya.summary: Eleventh and last Emir of the Aghlabids in Ifriqiya, who ruled from 903 to 909 and died between 911 and 916.

ishaq-ibn-imran.name: Ishaq Ibn Imran
ishaq-ibn-imran.summary: Arab physician working in Kairouan (died c. 905) whose treatise on melancholy was later translated into Latin.

ibn-al-jazzar.name: Ibn al-Jazzar
ibn-al-jazzar.summary: A 10th-century Muslim physician from Qayrawan in Tunisia (895–979), famous for his writings on Islamic medicine and known in Europe by the Latinized name Algizar.

dunash-ibn-tamim.name: Dunash ibn Tamim
dunash-ibn-tamim.summary: Tenth-century Jewish scholar and physician at the Fatimid court in Kairouan, known for a commentary on the Sefer Yetzirah and works on astronomy.

ibrahim-ii-of-ifriqiya.name: Ibrahim II of Ifriqiya
ibrahim-ii-of-ifriqiya.summary: Emir of Ifriqiya from 875 until his abdication in 902, a centralizing ruler who improved public works and commerce but later developed a reputation for cruelty.

paul-of-aegina.name: Paul of Aegina
paul-of-aegina.summary: 7th-century Byzantine Greek physician best known for writing a seven-book medical encyclopedia that for centuries held the sum of medical knowledge in the Byzantine Empire.

justinian-i.name: Justinian I
justinian-i.summary: Roman emperor from 527 to 565 whose generals reconquered much of the former Western Roman Empire and who is remembered for his sweeping rewrite of Roman law.

al-walid-i.name: Al-Walid I
al-walid-i.summary: Sixth Umayyad caliph (705–715) who expanded the caliphate to its largest extent and built major mosques including the Great Mosque of Damascus.

ismailism.name: Ismailism
ismailism.summary: A denomination of Shia Islam, one of three alongside Twelver and Zaydi Islam, marked by its distinctive emphasis on the esoteric, hidden meaning of Islamic teaching.

musa-ibn-nusayr.name: Musa ibn Nusayr
musa-ibn-nusayr.summary: Arab Muslim military commander and Umayyad governor (c. 640–716) who completed the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb and oversaw the conquest of the Iberian Peninsula.

aur-s-mountains.name: Aurès Mountains
aur-s-mountains.summary: A subrange of the Saharan Atlas in northeastern Algeria that gives its name to the surrounding historical and natural region.

ghadames.name: Ghadames
ghadames.summary: Ancient oasis town in northwestern Libya, one of the oldest pre-Saharan settlements, known for its traditional multi-storey architecture.

praetorian-prefect.name: Praetorian prefect
praetorian-prefect.summary: A high Roman office established by Augustus in 2 BC, originally commander of the Praetorian Guard, which grew into the emperor's chief aide and later a top territorial administrator.

exarchate.name: Exarchate
exarchate.summary: A political or ecclesiastical administrative jurisdiction, historical or modern, headed by an official called an exarch.

maurice-emperor.name: Maurice
maurice-emperor.summary: Eastern Roman emperor from 582 to 602 and the last of the Justinian dynasty, a successful general who ended the war with Persia and campaigned extensively against the Avars in the Balkans; he lived 539–602.

garmul.name: Garmul
garmul.summary: A Berber king of the Mauro-Roman Kingdom known for military campaigns and raids against Byzantine rule in North Africa.

mauro-roman-kingdom.name: Mauro-Roman Kingdom
mauro-roman-kingdom.summary: A Christian Berber kingdom, also called the Kingdom of Masuna, that dominated Roman Mauretania Caesariensis from its capital Altava as Roman control in the region weakened in the 5th century.

kingdom-of-altava.name: Kingdom of Altava
kingdom-of-altava.summary: An independent Christian Berber kingdom centered on the city of Altava in what is now northern Algeria, formed after the collapse of the Mauro-Roman Kingdom and lasting until the Umayyad conquest.

sulaymanid-dynasty.name: Sulaymanid dynasty
sulaymanid-dynasty.summary: Arab Muslim dynasty that ruled part of present-day western Algeria from 814 to 922, founded by Sulayman I, brother of Fez's founder Idris I.

sulayman-i-of-tlemcen.name: Sulayman I
sulayman-i-of-tlemcen.summary: Founder of the Sulaymanid dynasty in Algeria and brother of Idris I of Morocco; probably born around 730 and died in 814, having governed Tlemcen from around 786, according to the historians Sénac and Cressier.

hasan-ibn-ali.name: Hasan ibn Ali
hasan-ibn-ali.summary: Eldest grandson of the Islamic prophet Muhammad and eldest son of Ali and Fatima, who briefly served as caliph in 661 before ceding power to Mu'awiya, and is the second Shia Imam.

abu-al-muhajir-dinar.name: Abu al-Muhajir Dinar
abu-al-muhajir-dinar.summary: Umayyad governor of Ifriqiya who led the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb and died in 683 after the Battle of Vescera.

biskra.name: Biskra
biskra.summary: The main city of Algeria's Zibans region, at the edge of the Sahara, crossed over the centuries by Romans, Arabs and the French.

kusaila.name: Kusaila
kusaila.summary: A 7th-century Berber Christian ruler of the kingdom of Altava who led Berber resistance to the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb, winning a major victory in 683 before being killed in battle in 688.

talkata.name: Talkata
talkata.summary: A sedentary Sanhaja tribe of the central Maghreb during the Middle Ages, whose leaders founded the Zirid dynasty that ruled the region, Ifriqiya, and Al-Andalus.

ziri-ibn-manad.name: Ziri ibn Manad
ziri-ibn-manad.summary: Berber chief who founded the Zirid dynasty in the Maghreb, building the fortress of Achir in 935 and conquering Fez in 959, before dying in battle in 971.

achir.name: Achir
achir.summary: Medieval Berber city in Algeria's Titteri Mountains, founded in 935 as the first capital of the Zirid dynasty under Fatimid rule.

battle-of-carthage-698.name: Battle of Carthage (698)
battle-of-carthage-698.summary: A 698 battle in which Umayyad forces defeated a Byzantine expeditionary army, ending Byzantine resistance and clearing the way for the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb.

beni-guil.name: Beni Guil
beni-guil.summary: A mostly nomadic Bedouin Arab tribe in eastern Morocco, granted grazing rights in the 10th century by the Fatimid caliph and still the region's largest livestock farmers.

ibn-khaldun.name: Ibn Khaldun
ibn-khaldun.summary: An Arab Tunisian scholar and historian (1332–1406), best known for the Muqaddimah, a foundational work in historiography, sociology and economics.

zuhayr-ibn-qays.name: Zuhayr ibn Qays
zuhayr-ibn-qays.summary: Arab commander and companion of Muhammad, who led early Muslim conquests in Egypt, Barqa and Ifriqiya before being killed by Byzantine raiders in 688.

battle-of-mamma.name: Battle of Mamma
battle-of-mamma.summary: Battle fought around 686 to 690 CE in which Umayyad Arab forces defeated Berber king Caecilius of Altava, who was killed despite Byzantine support.

berber-languages.name: Berber languages
berber-languages.summary: A branch of the Afroasiatic language family, also called Tamazight or Amazigh, spoken by indigenous Berber communities across North Africa, mainly in Morocco and Algeria.

heraclius-the-elder.name: Heraclius the Elder
heraclius-the-elder.summary: Byzantine general and father of Emperor Heraclius who, around 608, rebelled with his son against the usurper Phocas, helping his son take the imperial throne.

phocas.name: Phocas
phocas.summary: Eastern Roman emperor from 602 to 610 who rose from the army to overthrow Emperor Maurice, and was himself overthrown and executed by Heraclius.

heraclius.name: Heraclius
heraclius.summary: Byzantine emperor from 610 to 641 who seized power in a revolt against Phocas, then fought long wars against Persia and the Arabs, driving the Persians from Asia Minor before losing territory to Arab conquests.

muslim-conquest-of-the-maghreb.name: Muslim conquest of the Maghreb
muslim-conquest-of-the-maghreb.summary: Nearly 70-year campaign (647-709) in which the Rashidun and Umayyad Caliphates conquered Byzantine North Africa, ending Byzantine rule in the Maghreb under Caliph al-Walid I.

al-kindi.name: Al-Kindi
al-kindi.summary: A Mesopotamian Arab polymath (c. 801-873) hailed as the 'father of Arab philosophy,' who oversaw the translation of Greek texts at Baghdad's House of Wisdom and wrote on subjects from mathematics to medicine.

islamic-philosophy.name: Falsafa
islamic-philosophy.summary: One of two Arabic terms for philosophy in the Islamic tradition, covering philosophy, logic, mathematics and physics, distinct from kalam, a rationalist theology.

kalam.name: Kalam
kalam.summary: The scholastic, rational study of Islamic theology, developed to defend Islamic beliefs against philosophical doubters, which rose to prominence under schools such as the Mu'tazilites, Ash'aris and Maturidis.

archdiocese-of-carthage.name: Church of Carthage
archdiocese-of-carthage.summary: The Christian diocese founded in Carthage in the 2nd century AD, the leading centre of Christianity in Roman Africa, whose figures included Church Fathers Tertullian and Cyprian.

mohamed-talbi.name: Mohamed Talbi
mohamed-talbi.summary: Tunisian author, professor and Islamic scholar who lived from 1921 to 2017.

gabriel-camps.name: Gabriel Camps
gabriel-camps.summary: French archaeologist and social anthropologist (1927–2002) who founded the Encyclopédie berbère and is considered a leading scholar of Berber history.

m-hamed-hassine-fantar.name: M'hamed Hassine Fantar
m-hamed-hassine-fantar.summary: Tunisian professor of ancient history, archaeology and history of religion at Tunis University, born 1936.

donatism.name: Donatism
donatism.summary: A Christian schism in North Africa (4th–6th centuries) holding that clergy must be faultless for their sacraments to be valid, which blended Christianity with Berber customs.

donatus-magnus.name: Donatus Magnus
donatus-magnus.summary: A charismatic early 4th-century North African Christian leader who founded the Donatist movement following the Diocletianic Persecution.

banu-tamim.name: Banu Tamim
banu-tamim.summary: An Arab tribe originating in Najd and Hejaz, now present across the Middle East and with a strong presence in the Maghreb.

tlemcen.name: Tlemcen
tlemcen.summary: The second-largest city in northwestern Algeria, a historic center of the Maghreb blending Arab, Berber, Andalusi, and Ottoman influences.

b-ja-a.name: Béjaïa
b-ja-a.summary: A Mediterranean port city in Algeria, now capital of Béjaïa Province, built up from a small fishing village into a fortified town by the Hammadid emir al-Nasir starting in 1067.

atlas-mountains.name: Atlas Mountains
atlas-mountains.summary: Mountain range in the Maghreb stretching about 2,500 km through Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, separating the Sahara from the Mediterranean and Atlantic, and home mainly to Berber populations.
